nameStory: The swordfish gets its name from its most striking feature - a long, flat, pointed bill that looks exactly like a medieval sword blade. This incredible "sword" can make up nearly one-third of the fish's total body length, making it impossible to mistake for anything else in New England waters!
description: The swordfish is a massive ocean predator that's built like a living torpedo with a sword attached to its nose. These incredible fish can grow up to 10 feet long (with some giants reaching nearly 15 feet!) and are perfectly designed for life in the open ocean. By the time they're adults, swordfish have completely smooth, scaleless skin and no teeth - they rely entirely on that famous sword-like bill to hunt their prey.

idTips.label: Sword Bill
idTips.description: The unmistakable long, flat, pointed bill extends like a broadsword from the upper jaw, feeling rigid and bone-like if touched. This "sword" is typically dark on top and lighter underneath.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped body that feels incredibly firm and muscular, with a distinctive high dorsal fin that curves backward like a sail when the fish is fresh.

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Adult skin is completely smooth and scaleless, feeling almost rubbery to the touch, unlike the rough, sandpaper texture of many other large fish.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Enormous fish typically 6-10 feet long when caught in New England waters, with a hefty, dense body that can weigh several hundred pounds.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark metallic blue or blackish on top with a silvery-white belly, often with a slight iridescent sheen that's most noticeable when the fish is freshly caught.

habitat: Swordfish are found in the deep, open waters off New England's continental shelf, typically 20+ miles offshore in waters over 600 feet deep. They're highly migratory ocean wanderers that follow warm currents and can dive to extraordinary depths of over 1,800 feet while hunting. You'll never find them in shallow coastal waters, bays, or anywhere near shore.

seasonality.spring: Swordfish begin moving into New England's offshore waters as temperatures warm, following bait fish northward along the continental shelf edge.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for swordfish in New England waters, when they're most commonly caught by deep-sea fishing boats working the offshore canyons and seamounts.
seasonality.fall: Still present in offshore waters but beginning their southward migration as surface temperatures start to cool.
seasonality.winter: Rarely found in New England waters as they migrate south to warmer tropical and subtropical regions.

funFact: Swordfish have a built-in brain heater! They have special organs that warm their brain and eyes up to 28°F above the surrounding water temperature, giving them lightning-fast reflexes even in the frigid depths where they hunt.
confusionNotes: Swordfish are sometimes confused with marlin, but marlins have a round, spear-like bill (not flat like a sword) and keep their scales and teeth as adults. Remember: sword-FISH has a flat sword bill, while marlin has a round spear bill.
contextualKnowledge: While called "broadbill" in some places, this name isn't commonly used in New England - locals and fishermen almost always call them swordfish. These are the fish behind the famous Gloucester fishing story in "The Perfect Storm," highlighting their importance to New England's deep-sea fishing industry.
compareHints: Swordfish are the only member of their family (Xiphiidae), making them truly unique. The closest relatives are marlins and sailfish in the family Istiophoridae, but those fish have round bills instead of flat sword-like bills, and they retain their scales and teeth throughout their lives. Swordfish are the only billfish that completely loses both scales and teeth by adulthood.
